title: Mount Etna's secret origin: could it be a rare 'petit-spot' volcano?
summary: Mount Etna, Europe's most active volcano, has long defied easy explanation. Rising over 3,000 meters on Sicily, it erupts frequently yet doesn't fit neatly into the three standard volcano categories: divergent boundary, subduction zone, or hotspot. Now, researchers led by Sébastien Pilet at the University of Lausanne propose a radical new origin story: Etna may be a colossal example of a "petit-spot" volcano. Petit-spot volcanoes, first identified by Japanese geologists in 2006, are small submarine features formed when pre-existing magma pockets in the upper mantle are squeezed upward by tectonic plate flexure. The process resembles liquid being wrung from a sponge. Pilet's team argues that the collision between the African and Eurasian plates beneath Sicily creates fractures that allow such magma—sitting about 80 kilometers deep—to rise and feed Etna. This would explain both the volcano's unusual lava chemistry, which resembles hotspot magmas despite no hotspot being present, and its remarkably stable composition over 500,000 years. The researchers analyzed rock samples spanning Etna's history and found that the magma's chemical signature has remained consistent, supporting a steady, plate-driven supply rather than episodic melting. "This is unexpected, as such processes had previously only been observed in very small volcanic structures, typically rising no more than a few hundred meters," said Pilet. If confirmed, Mount Etna would be the first known giant petit-spot volcano, potentially opening a new chapter in volcanology. The findings, published in the Journal of Geophysical Research—Solid Earth, could also refine volcanic hazard assessments for the densely populated region around Catania. The study encourages scientists to search for similar formations elsewhere, suggesting that Earth's volcanic diversity may be greater than currently recognized.
why_it_matters: A new volcano-forming mechanism means our risk maps for earthquakes and eruptions may need updating. For communities living near volcanoes that don't fit the textbook mold, this research could lead to better preparation and warning systems, potentially saving lives and property.

background_read: Most volcanoes are born in three settings: where tectonic plates pull apart (divergent boundaries like Iceland), where one plate dives under another (subduction zones like the Ring of Fire around the Pacific), or above especially hot columns of upwelling mantle (hotspots like Hawaii). But some volcanoes—like Mount Etna—sit in complicated plate collision zones and don't neatly match these.

The concept of petit-spot volcanoes was introduced in 2006 when Japanese geologists found tiny seamounts on the Pacific plate where it bends before diving into the Japan Trench. The bending squeezes up blobs of old magma from the shallow mantle, creating small, scattered eruptions. Before now, no one imagined this mechanism could build a giant like Etna.

Etna rises over 3,300 meters and has been documented erupting for thousands of years. The ancient Greeks believed it was the forge of the god Hephaestus. Its frequent ash and lava flows pose a direct threat to the city of Catania and its surrounding infrastructure, making hazard models a matter of public safety.

By analyzing the unchanging chemistry of Etna's lavas over half a million years, researchers found it matched the continuous supply expected from a flexure-driven system rather than sporadic deep melting. If confirmed, this would rewrite the textbooks on how large, persistent volcanoes can form.

perspectives.description: If Mount Etna is indeed a giant petit-spot volcano, it shows that our planet still holds geological secrets, opening an entirely new category of volcanic systems. This could inspire young geologists to look for similar giants in unexpected places and deepen our knowledge of Earth's interior.

Skeptics note that the idea stretches a mechanism observed only in tiny seamounts to one of the world's largest active volcanoes. More geophysical data—like seismic tomography of the deep plumbing system—will be needed before overthrowing decades of established models.

Volcanology's history is full of unexpected discoveries: plate tectonics itself was resisted for decades. The petit-spot hypothesis fits a pattern where anomalies in lava chemistry force scientists to reconsider fundamental assumptions, driving the field forward through debate and new observations.

If verified, the research will likely spur targeted seafloor surveys and satellite-based deformation measurements around other odd volcanoes worldwide. Improved hazard models could then integrate the flexure-squeeze mechanism, providing more accurate eruption forecasts for Etna and similar settings, from Chile to Japan.
